sections.title: Werner's two valences: the wedding-stage picture

board_events.text: A metal satisfies TWO kinds of demand at once
Picture an Indian wedding: the groom is fixed at the centre, a tight inner circle of family locked around him, while well-wishers drift freely in the parking area.

board_events.text: The $primary$ valence is the metal's ionisable charge $-$ what we now call its oxidation number $-$ satisfied by ions sitting outside.
Secondary valence = fixed positions right around the metal = the coordination number
Those secondary-valence positions point in definite directions in space, so they fix the shape of the whole complex.
Alfred Werner saw all this in the eighteen nineties, and won the Nobel Prize in nineteen thirteen for it.
Get these two valences straight and the entire chapter has somewhere firm to stand.

segments.text: <curious>Here is the big idea.</curious> A metal quietly satisfies two completely different kinds of demand at the same time.
Think of a busy Indian wedding. The groom sits fixed at the centre, a tight inner circle of family locked around him, while the well-wishers outside just drift in and out freely.
Look at the picture: a metal at the centre, a bonded inner sphere gripping it, and loose counter ions floating outside.
The first demand is the primary valence. That is simply the metal's ionisable charge, what we now call its oxidation number, and it is satisfied by ions sitting outside the inner circle.
The second demand is the secondary valence: a fixed number of positions right around the metal, which is what we now call the coordination number.
These positions point in definite directions in space, and that is exactly what fixes the shape of the whole complex.
Alfred Werner worked all this out back in the eighteen nineties, and it earned him the Nobel Prize in nineteen thirteen.
Once these two valences are clear in your head, <excited>the entire chapter finally has somewhere firm to stand.</excited>
<curious>तो सोचो</curious> एक metal दो अलग तरह की demand एक साथ satisfy करता है।
एक busy Indian wedding imagine करो: groom बीच में fixed बैठा है, close family का एक tight inner circle उसके around locked है, और well-wishers बाहर parking में freely घूम रहे हैं।
यहाँ picture में देखो: बीच में metal, उसके around bonded inner sphere, और बाहर free counter ions.
पहली demand है primary valence, यानी metal का ionisable charge, जिसे आज हम oxidation number कहते हैं, और ये बाहर बैठे ions से satisfy होता है।
दूसरी demand है secondary valence, यानी metal के बिलकुल around fixed positions, जिन्हें हम coordination number कहते हैं।
ये positions space में definite directions में point करती हैं, और यही पूरे complex का shape decide करती हैं।
Alfred Werner ने ये सब eighteen nineties में समझ लिया था, और इसके लिए उन्हें nineteen thirteen में Nobel Prize मिला।
ये दोनों valences clear हो जाएँ, तो <excited>पूरा chapter एक solid base पर खड़ा हो जाता है।</excited>

sections.title: The experimental proof: silver nitrate and conductivity

board_events.text: How do we KNOW there are two zones?
Take cobalt$-$ammonia chlorides of the same metal, dissolve each in water, add silver nitrate, and count the chloride that instantly falls out as silver chloride.

board_events.caption: Chlorides that ionise fall as ammonia content drops

board_events.text: The chlorides that precipitate at once are the free, ionisable counter ions $-$ the primary valence.
The chlorides that stubbornly refuse to precipitate are locked in the inner circle and simply not available.
As the ammonia count falls from six down to four, the precipitated chloride drops in lockstep from three to one $-$ a clean, repeatable pattern.
Molar conductivity tells the same story: more free ions means better conduction
Two independent measurements, one conclusion $-$ there really are two zones around the metal.

segments.text: <curious>But how did anyone actually know</curious> there were two different zones around the metal?
You take a series of cobalt ammonia chlorides of the same metal, dissolve each one in water, add silver nitrate, and count how much chloride instantly drops out as silver chloride.
Watch the pattern in the chart: as the ammonia content falls, the amount of chloride that ionises falls right along with it.
The chlorides that precipitate at once are the free, ionisable counter ions. These are the ones satisfying the primary valence.
The chlorides that stubbornly refuse to come out are locked inside the inner circle, and are simply not available to react.
As the ammonia count drops from six down to four, the precipitated chloride falls in lockstep from three down to one. That clean, repeatable pattern is the clue.
Molar conductivity tells exactly the same story: the more free ions a solution releases, the better it conducts.
Two completely independent measurements, and they point to one conclusion: there really are two zones around the metal.
<curious>पर सवाल ये है</curious> कि हमें पता कैसे चला कि metal के around दो अलग zones हैं?
same metal के cobalt ammonia chlorides की एक series लो, हर एक को water में dissolve करो, silver nitrate डालो, और गिनो कि कितना chloride तुरंत silver chloride बनकर गिरता है।
chart में pattern देखो: जैसे-जैसे ammonia कम होता है, ionise होने वाला chloride भी उतना ही कम होता जाता है।
जो chlorides तुरंत precipitate होते हैं, वो free ionisable counter ions हैं, यही primary valence satisfy करते हैं।
और जो chlorides precipitate होने से मना कर देते हैं, वो inner circle में locked हैं, इसलिए react करने के लिए available ही नहीं हैं।
जैसे ammonia six से घटकर four होता है, precipitate होने वाला chloride भी three से घटकर one हो जाता है, बिलकुल lockstep में।
Molar conductivity भी बिलकुल यही कहानी बताती है: जितने ज़्यादा free ions, उतनी अच्छी conduction.
दो बिलकुल अलग measurements, और दोनों एक ही conclusion देते हैं: metal के around सच में दो zones हैं।

sections.title: Double salt versus complex: seeing the fence

board_events.text: What a coordination compound is NOT
Dissolve potash alum or Mohr's salt and it disintegrates completely into all its simple ions, each giving its ordinary chemical test $-$ these are double salts.

board_events.text: Potassium ferrocyanide refuses to do this: in water it releases potassium but keeps the iron$-$cyanide unit intact, so there is no free iron test and no free cyanide test.
The square bracket in the formula is a fence: whatever is inside is the bonded coordination sphere that travels as one unit; whatever is outside is a free counter ion.
The pieces inside are ligands $-$ ions or molecules that donate a lone pair. In Lewis terms the ligand is the base and the metal is the acid.
Ammonium cannot be a ligand $-$ its lone pair is already busy holding the fourth hydrogen
Transition metals are perfect acceptors because they have low$-$lying vacant d$-$orbitals waiting to receive those pairs.

segments.text: It really helps to first pin down what a coordination compound is not.
Dissolve potash alum, or Mohr's salt, and it falls apart completely into all its simple ions, and each ion gives its ordinary chemical test. These are called double salts.
Look at the contrast: the double salt breaks into everything, but a genuine complex keeps an inner unit together.
Potassium ferrocyanide refuses to fall apart. In water it releases potassium, but it keeps the iron and cyanide unit intact, so you get no free iron test and no free cyanide test.
The square bracket in the formula is really a fence. Whatever is inside is the bonded coordination sphere that travels as one unit; whatever is outside is a free counter ion.
The pieces inside the fence are the ligands: ions or molecules that donate a lone pair. In Lewis language the ligand is the base and the central metal is the acid.
Notice that ammonium cannot be a ligand, because nitrogen's lone pair is already busy holding on to the fourth hydrogen.
Transition metals make perfect acceptors, because they have low lying vacant d orbitals just waiting to receive those donated pairs.
सबसे पहले ये समझना ज़रूरी है कि coordination compound क्या नहीं होता।
potash alum या Mohr's salt को dissolve करो तो ये पूरी तरह अपने simple ions में टूट जाते हैं, और हर ion अपना normal chemical test देता है। इन्हें double salts कहते हैं।
contrast देखो: double salt सब कुछ में टूट जाता है, पर एक genuine complex अपना inner unit एक साथ बचाकर रखता है।
Potassium ferrocyanide टूटने से मना कर देता है। water में ये potassium छोड़ता है पर iron और cyanide का unit intact रखता है, इसलिए ना free iron test आता है ना free cyanide test.
formula का square bracket दरअसल एक fence है। अंदर जो है वो bonded coordination sphere है जो एक unit की तरह travel करता है, और बाहर जो है वो free counter ion है।
fence के अंदर के pieces ligands हैं: ions या molecules जो एक lone pair donate करते हैं। Lewis language में ligand base है और central metal acid.
ध्यान दो, ammonium ligand नहीं बन सकता, क्योंकि nitrogen का lone pair पहले से चौथे hydrogen को पकड़ने में लगा है।
Transition metals perfect acceptors बनते हैं, क्योंकि उनके पास low lying vacant d orbitals होते हैं जो ये donated pairs receive करने के लिए ready रहते हैं।

sections.title: Ligands and denticity: count arms, not ligands

board_events.text: Denticity: how many donor atoms one ligand uses
A unidentate ligand binds through one donor atom $-$ chloride, water, ammonia, cyanide.

board_events.text: A didentate ligand binds through two donor atoms at once $-$ ethane one two diamine, called en, plus oxalate and glycinate.
A polydentate ligand uses several: dien uses three, trien uses four, and E D T A is hexadentate, gripping through two nitrogen and four oxygen atoms.
An ambidentate ligand has two different possible donors but uses only one at a time $-$ nitrite through nitrogen or oxygen, thiocyanate through sulphur or nitrogen.
Ambidentate is NOT didentate: one donor used at a time, versus both used together
A di$-$ or polydentate ligand that closes a ring is a chelate; such rings, especially five$-$ and six$-$membered ones, make the complex far more stable $-$ the chelate effect.

segments.text: Denticity answers one question: how many donor atoms does a single ligand use to grip one metal?
A unidentate ligand binds through just one donor atom. Chloride, water, ammonia and cyanide are the everyday examples.
Look at how the different ligands grip the metal: one holds with a single arm, another with two, another wraps around with several.
A didentate ligand binds through two donor atoms at once. Ethane one two diamine, which we call en, along with oxalate and glycinate, are the standard cases.
A polydentate ligand uses several donor atoms: dien uses three, trien uses four, and E D T A is hexadentate, gripping through two nitrogen and four oxygen atoms.
An ambidentate ligand is different: it has two possible donor atoms but uses only one at a time. Nitrite can bind through nitrogen or oxygen, and thiocyanate through sulphur or nitrogen.
<curious>Here is a distinction students blur:</curious> ambidentate is not didentate. Ambidentate uses one donor at a time, while didentate uses both together.
A di or polydentate ligand that closes a ring is called a chelate, and such rings, especially five and six membered ones, make the complex far more stable. That extra stability is the chelate effect.
Denticity एक सवाल का जवाब देती है: एक single ligand कितने donor atoms use करके एक metal को पकड़ता है?
Unidentate ligand सिर्फ एक donor atom से बंधता है। Chloride, water, ammonia और cyanide इसके रोज़मर्रा के examples हैं।
देखो अलग-अलग ligands metal को कैसे पकड़ते हैं: कोई एक arm से, कोई दो से, कोई कई arms से wrap कर लेता है।
Didentate ligand एक साथ दो donor atoms से बंधता है। Ethane one two diamine, जिसे हम en कहते हैं, oxalate और glycinate इसके standard cases हैं।
Polydentate ligand कई donor atoms use करता है: dien तीन, trien चार, और E D T A hexadentate है, दो nitrogen और चार oxygen से पकड़ता है।
Ambidentate ligand अलग है: इसके पास दो possible donor atoms होते हैं पर एक बार में एक ही use होता है। Nitrite nitrogen या oxygen से बंध सकता है, और thiocyanate sulphur या nitrogen से।
<curious>यहाँ एक distinction है जो students अक्सर मिला देते हैं:</curious> ambidentate, didentate नहीं है। Ambidentate एक बार में एक donor use करता है, जबकि didentate दोनों एक साथ।
जो di या polydentate ligand ring बनाकर बंधता है उसे chelate कहते हैं, और ऐसी rings, खासकर five और six membered, complex को बहुत ज़्यादा stable बनाती हैं। यही extra stability chelate effect है।

board_events.text: The coordination sphere is the metal plus its attached ligands, written inside square brackets; ionisable groups written outside are counter ions.
One coordination number can give more than one shape $-$ four can be tetrahedral or square planar $-$ so geometry must be stated in its own right, never just read off the number.
The oxidation number is the charge the metal would carry if every ligand were removed with its shared pair, written as a Roman numeral.
A homoleptic complex has only one kind of donor group; a heteroleptic complex has more than one kind.
Coordination number counts sigma donors only $-$ pi bonds and counter ions never count

segments.text: Now let us gather the rest of the vocabulary. Think of this as the naming toolkit.
The coordination number is the count of sigma donor atoms bonded directly to the metal, and the common values you will meet are two, four and six.
Look at these shapes: one central atom can sit in a linear, a tetrahedral, a square planar, or an octahedral arrangement.
The coordination sphere is the metal together with its attached ligands, written inside square brackets, while any ionisable groups written outside are the counter ions.
A single coordination number can give more than one shape. Four can be tetrahedral or square planar, so you must state the geometry in its own right, never just read it off the number.
The oxidation number is the charge the metal would carry if every ligand were pulled away with its shared pair, and we write it as a Roman numeral.
A homoleptic complex has only one kind of donor group, while a heteroleptic complex has more than one kind.
Remember, the coordination number counts sigma donors only. Pi bonds and counter ions never count towards it.
अब बाकी की vocabulary इकट्ठा करते हैं। इसे naming का toolkit समझो।
Coordination number है metal से directly bonded sigma donor atoms की गिनती, और common values जो मिलेंगे वो हैं two, four और six.
ये shapes देखो: एक central atom linear, tetrahedral, square planar, या octahedral arrangement में बैठ सकता है।
Coordination sphere है metal plus उसके attached ligands, square brackets के अंदर, और बाहर लिखे कोई भी ionisable groups counter ions हैं।
एक ही coordination number एक से ज़्यादा shape दे सकता है। Four tetrahedral भी हो सकता है square planar भी, इसलिए geometry हमेशा अलग से बतानी पड़ती है, सिर्फ number से नहीं पढ़ी जाती।
Oxidation number वो charge है जो metal पर होता अगर हर ligand अपने shared pair के साथ हटा दिया जाए, और इसे हम Roman numeral में लिखते हैं।
Homoleptic complex में सिर्फ एक तरह का donor group होता है, जबकि heteroleptic में एक से ज़्यादा।
याद रखो, coordination number सिर्फ sigma donors गिनता है। Pi bonds और counter ions इसमें कभी count नहीं होते।

sections.title: Two relations that do all the bookkeeping

board_events.text: Charge balance and coordination number
Rearranged, this is your everyday tool for finding the metal's oxidation state: neutral ligands like ammonia and water contribute zero, anionic ligands contribute their own charge.
So two oxalate ions, each didentate, contribute two times two, which is four to the coordination number $-$ not two.
To write a name from a formula: cation first, then ligands alphabetically before the metal; anionic ligand names end in oh, and simple ligands take di, tri, tetra.
If the complex ion is an anion, the metal takes the suffix ate, often with a Latin stem: ferrate, cuprate, argentate, plumbate, stannate, aurate

segments.text: This sub-topic has two genuine quantitative tools, and they do all the bookkeeping.
The first: the charge on the complex ion equals the oxidation number of the metal plus the sum of all the ligand charges.
Rearranged, this is your everyday tool for the metal's oxidation state. Neutral ligands like ammonia and water contribute zero, while anionic ligands contribute their own charge.
The second: the coordination number equals the sum, over each ligand, of the number of ligands times its denticity.
So two oxalate ions, each one didentate, contribute two times two, which is four towards the coordination number, and not just two.
To write a name from a formula: the cation comes first, then the ligands alphabetically before the metal. Anionic ligand names end in oh, and simple ligands take di, tri or tetra.
And if the complex ion is an anion, the metal takes the suffix ate, often with a Latin stem, such as ferrate, cuprate, argentate, plumbate, stannate or aurate.
Watch how the name potassium hexacyanidoferrate three reads straight off the formula, one rule at a time.
इस sub-topic के दो असली quantitative tools हैं, और यही सारी bookkeeping करते हैं।
पहला: complex ion का charge बराबर है metal का oxidation number plus सारे ligand charges का sum.
इसे rearrange करके हम metal का oxidation state निकालते हैं। Neutral ligands जैसे ammonia और water zero contribute करते हैं, और anionic ligands अपना खुद का charge।
दूसरा: coordination number बराबर है हर ligand के लिए, ligands की संख्या गुना उसकी denticity, का sum.
तो दो oxalate ions, हर एक didentate, देते हैं two into two यानी four coordination number को, सिर्फ two नहीं।
formula से name लिखने के लिए: पहले cation, फिर ligands alphabetically metal से पहले। Anionic ligand names oh पर खत्म होते हैं, और simple ligands पर di, tri या tetra लगता है।
और अगर complex ion anion है तो metal पर ate suffix लगता है, अक्सर Latin stem के साथ, जैसे ferrate, cuprate, argentate, plumbate, stannate या aurate.
देखो कैसे name potassium hexacyanidoferrate three सीधे formula से पढ़ा जाता है, एक-एक rule से।

board_events.text: We are given a complex with four ammine and two chlorido ligands inside the sphere, and one chloride sitting outside.
That single outside chloride is the counter ion, so the complex ion itself must carry a charge of plus one.
The coordination number is four plus two, which is six, since all six ligands are unidentate.
For the name, ligands go alphabetically $-$ ammine before chlorido $-$ and because the metal is in a cation it is named as the element with a Roman numeral.
Name: tetraamminedichloridochromium(III) chloride

segments.text: In this example we name the compound, and then find the oxidation number and coordination number of chromium.
Look at the structure: four ammine and two chlorido ligands sit inside the sphere, and one chloride sits outside.
So we are given four ammine and two chlorido ligands inside the sphere, with one chloride outside.
That single outside chloride is the counter ion, which means the complex ion itself must carry a charge of plus one.
Setting it up: x plus four times zero plus two times minus one equals plus one, so x comes out as plus three.
The coordination number is four plus two, which is six, since all six of these ligands are unidentate.
For the name, the ligands go alphabetically, ammine before chlorido, and because the metal sits in a cation it is named as the element with a Roman numeral.
The full name is tetraamminedichloridochromium three chloride.
इस example में हम compound को name करते हैं, फिर chromium का oxidation number और coordination number निकालते हैं।
structure देखो: चार ammine और दो chlorido ligands sphere के अंदर हैं, और एक chloride बाहर।
तो हमें दिया है चार ammine और दो chlorido ligands sphere के अंदर, और एक chloride बाहर।
वो अकेला बाहर वाला chloride counter ion है, इसका मतलब complex ion खुद plus one charge रखता होगा।
Set up करते हैं: x plus four into zero plus two into minus one बराबर plus one, तो x निकलता है plus three.
Coordination number है four plus two यानी six, क्योंकि ये छहों ligands unidentate हैं।
Name के लिए ligands alphabetically आते हैं, ammine पहले chlorido बाद में, और metal cation में है इसलिए element के नाम से Roman numeral के साथ लिखा जाता है।
पूरा name है tetraamminedichloridochromium three chloride.

sections.title: Worked example: the silver-nitrate speed trap

board_events.text: The AgCl count tells you the fence position instantly
A cobalt(III) chloride$-$ammonia solid has composition cobalt chloride with five ammonia; treating one mole with excess silver nitrate gives exactly two moles of silver chloride.
Speed logic: moles of silver chloride equal moles of ionisable chloride, which equals the chloride sitting outside the bracket $-$ here that is two.
So two chlorides are counter ions, and the remaining one chloride plus all five ammonia sit inside.

board_events.text: Coordination formula: [Co(NH3)5Cl]Cl2, coordination number six
The coordination number is five plus one, which is six.
The lazy reflex is three chlorine so three silver chloride $-$ wrong; only the outside chlorides ionise. Read the precipitate count first.

segments.text: Here is a favourite N E E T speed trap, where the silver chloride count instantly tells you the fence position.
A cobalt three chloride ammonia solid has the composition cobalt chloride with five ammonia. When one mole is treated with excess silver nitrate, exactly two moles of silver chloride precipitate.
The speed logic is this: moles of silver chloride equal moles of ionisable chloride, which equals the chloride sitting outside the bracket, and here that number is two.
So two chlorides are the counter ions, and the remaining one chloride together with all five ammonia sit inside the coordination sphere.
Look at the picture: two chlorides outside as counter ions, one chloride and five ammonia inside.
That gives the coordination formula: cobalt with five ammonia and one chloride inside the bracket, two chloride outside, coordination number six.
The coordination number itself is five plus one, which is six.
<chuckle>The lazy reflex is</chuckle> three chlorine in the formula so three silver chloride. That is wrong. Only the outside chlorides ionise, so always read the precipitate count first.
ये एक favourite N E E T speed trap है, जहाँ silver chloride की count तुरंत fence की position बता देती है।

एक cobalt three chloride ammonia solid की composition है cobalt chloride with five ammonia. जब एक mole को excess silver nitrate से treat करते हैं, exactly two moles silver chloride precipitate होता है।
Speed logic ये है: silver chloride के moles बराबर हैं ionisable chloride के moles, यानी bracket के बाहर बैठा chloride, और यहाँ वो number two है।
तो दो chlorides counter ions हैं, और बाकी एक chloride plus सारे पाँच ammonia coordination sphere के अंदर बैठे हैं।
picture देखो: दो chloride बाहर counter ions की तरह, एक chloride और पाँच ammonia अंदर।
इससे coordination formula मिलता है: cobalt with five ammonia and one chloride bracket के अंदर, दो chloride बाहर, coordination number six.
Coordination number खुद है five plus one यानी six.
<chuckle>lazy reflex ये है</chuckle> कि formula में तीन chlorine तो तीन silver chloride। ये गलत है। सिर्फ बाहर वाले chlorides ionise होते हैं, इसलिए हमेशा पहले precipitate count पढ़ो।

One potassium sits outside, so the complex ion carries a charge of minus one.

segments.text: This J E E Main example brings denticity, oxidation number and anionic naming together in one shot.
Inside the sphere sit one en, which is neutral and didentate, and two oxalate ions, each carrying a charge of minus two and each didentate.
One potassium sits outside the bracket, so the complex ion must carry a charge of minus one.
Setting up the oxidation number: x plus zero plus two times minus two equals minus one, so x comes out as plus three.
For the coordination number, en contributes one times two, and oxalate contributes two times two, which together give six.
Look at the picture: one en ring and two oxalate rings clamp the cobalt, three chelate rings giving coordination number six.
For the name, because the complex is an anion the metal becomes cobaltate three, and the ligands go alphabetically, ethane one two diamine before oxalato.
The full name is potassium, ethane one two diamine, dioxalatocobaltate three.
ये J E E Main example denticity, oxidation number और anionic naming तीनों को एक साथ लाता है।
sphere के अंदर एक en है जो neutral और didentate है, और दो oxalate ions हैं, हर एक minus two charge का और didentate.
एक potassium bracket के बाहर है, इसलिए complex ion minus one charge रखता होगा।
oxidation number set up करते हैं: x plus zero plus two into minus two बराबर minus one, तो x निकलता है plus three.
Coordination number के लिए en देता है one into two, और oxalate देता है two into two, जो मिलकर छह बनते हैं।
picture देखो: एक en ring और दो oxalate rings cobalt को clamp करती हैं, तीन chelate rings coordination number six देती हैं।
Name के लिए, complex anion है इसलिए metal बनता है cobaltate three, और ligands alphabetically आते हैं, ethane one two diamine पहले oxalato बाद में।
पूरा name है potassium, ethane one two diamine, dioxalatocobaltate three.

sections.title: Worked example: counter-ion reasoning, the A/B twins

board_events.text: Same formula, different inner sphere

Two solids A and B share the composition chromium with five water, one sulphate and one bromide. With silver nitrate, A gives a pale$-$yellow precipitate and B gives none; with barium chloride, A gives none and B gives a white one.
A pale$-$yellow precipitate with silver nitrate is silver bromide, so in A the bromide is the ionisable counter ion, which means the sulphate must be locked inside.

board_events.text: A white precipitate with barium chloride is barium sulphate, so in B the sulphate is the counter ion and the bromide is coordinated inside.
Both are chromium three with coordination number six $-$ identical composition, yet they precipitate different ions because a different group sits inside. That is pure Werner.

segments.text: This J E E Advanced example is pure counter-ion reasoning, straight from Werner's model.

Two solids A and B share the composition chromium with five water, one sulphate and one bromide. With silver nitrate, A gives a pale yellow precipitate and B gives none; with barium chloride, A gives none and B gives a white one.
A pale yellow precipitate with silver nitrate is silver bromide, so in A the bromide is the ionisable counter ion, which means the sulphate must be locked inside the sphere.
Look at the two structures: A keeps the sulphate inside and bromide out, while B keeps the bromide inside and sulphate out.
For A: x plus five times zero plus minus two equals plus one, so x is plus three.
A white precipitate with barium chloride is barium sulphate, so in B the sulphate is the counter ion and the bromide is coordinated inside.
For B: x plus five times zero plus minus one equals plus two, so x is again plus three.
Both are chromium three with coordination number six. Identical composition, yet they precipitate different ions because a different group sits inside the fence. That is Werner in its purest form.
ये J E E Advanced example pure counter-ion reasoning है, सीधे Werner के model से।

दो solids A और B की composition एक ही है: chromium with five water, one sulphate और one bromide. Silver nitrate से A pale yellow precipitate देता है B कुछ नहीं; barium chloride से A कुछ नहीं देता B white देता है।
Silver nitrate के साथ pale yellow precipitate silver bromide है, तो A में bromide ionisable counter ion है, यानी sulphate ज़रूर sphere के अंदर locked होगा।
दोनों structures देखो: A sulphate अंदर और bromide बाहर रखता है, जबकि B bromide अंदर और sulphate बाहर।
A के लिए: x plus five into zero plus minus two बराबर plus one, तो x है plus three.
Barium chloride के साथ white precipitate barium sulphate है, तो B में sulphate counter ion है और bromide अंदर coordinated है।
B के लिए: x plus five into zero plus minus one बराबर plus two, तो x फिर से plus three.
दोनों chromium three हैं coordination number six के साथ। Composition same है, फिर भी अलग ions precipitate होते हैं क्योंकि fence के अंदर अलग group बैठा है। ये Werner का सबसे pure रूप है।

sections.title: Pitfalls and pro-tips for Werner and naming

board_events.text: Where students bleed marks
The commonest slip is counting ligands instead of donor atoms for the coordination number; with chelating ligands you must multiply by denticity, so three oxalates give six, not three.
Only sigma$-$donor atoms inside the bracket count $-$ a chloride written outside adds to oxidation number, never to coordination number
Do not confuse ambidentate with didentate: ambidentate offers a choice of donor and uses one, while didentate uses both at once.

Watch the naming slips $-$ alphabetise by the ligand name not the multiplier, remember bis and tris for complex ligand names, and never forget the ate suffix with its Latin stem for anionic complexes.
Pro$-$tip for any silver$-$nitrate problem: the moles of precipitate equal the ionisable chlorides outside the bracket $-$ read that number, place those ions outside, everything else goes in.
A fast sanity check on any oxidation number: rebuild the complex$-$ion charge from your answer; if it does not match the counter$-$ion charge, you dropped a sign on a ligand.

segments.text: Let us close this sub-topic by looking at exactly where students lose marks.
The most common slip is counting ligands instead of donor atoms for the coordination number. With chelating ligands you must multiply by denticity, so three oxalates give six, not three.
Remember, only the sigma donor atoms inside the bracket count. A chloride written outside adds to the oxidation number, never to the coordination number.
Do not confuse ambidentate with didentate. Ambidentate offers a choice of donor atom and uses one, while didentate uses both of its donors at once.

Watch the naming slips: alphabetise by the ligand name, not by the multiplier, remember bis and tris for complex ligand names, and never forget the ate suffix with its Latin stem for anionic complexes.
A pro tip for any silver nitrate problem: the moles of precipitate equal the ionisable chlorides outside the bracket. Read that number, place those ions outside, and everything else goes in.
And a fast sanity check on any oxidation number: rebuild the complex ion charge from your answer. If it does not match the counter ion charge, you have dropped a sign on one of the ligands.
इस sub-topic को खत्म करते हैं ये देखकर कि students exactly कहाँ marks गँवाते हैं।
सबसे common slip है coordination number के लिए ligands गिनना, donor atoms नहीं। Chelating ligands के साथ denticity से multiply करना पड़ता है, तो तीन oxalates छह देते हैं, तीन नहीं।
याद रखो, सिर्फ bracket के अंदर के sigma donor atoms count होते हैं। बाहर लिखा chloride oxidation number में जुड़ता है, coordination number में कभी नहीं।
Ambidentate को didentate से confuse मत करो। Ambidentate donor atom का choice देता है और एक use करता है, जबकि didentate अपने दोनों donors एक साथ use करता है।

Naming slips पर ध्यान दो: ligand name से alphabetise करो multiplier से नहीं, complex ligand names के लिए bis और tris याद रखो, और anionic complexes के लिए ate suffix अपने Latin stem के साथ कभी मत भूलो।
किसी भी silver nitrate problem का pro tip: precipitate के moles बराबर हैं bracket के बाहर वाले ionisable chlorides। वो number पढ़ो, उतने ions बाहर रखो, बाकी सब अंदर।
और किसी भी oxidation number का fast check: अपने answer से complex ion का charge दोबारा बनाओ। अगर वो counter ion charge से match नहीं करता, तो किसी ligand पर sign छूट गया।

sections.title: Two families of isomers: the biryani and pulao split

board_events.text: Same formula, different arrangement
Two cooks get the exact same ingredients in the same amounts; one makes a biryani, the other a pulao $-$ same shopping list, different dish, different taste.
Isomers are exactly this: compounds with the same formula but a different arrangement of atoms, so their colour, melting point and reactivity all differ.
The whole zoo splits cleanly on one question: did the bonds change, or only the positions in space?

board_events.caption: Structural versus stereo, with their sub-types

board_events.text: Structural isomers have different bonds $-$ something moved between inside and outside the sphere, or a ligand is attached through a different atom.
Stereoisomers keep the same bonds but a different arrangement in space; nothing about what is bonded to what changes, only the geometry.
One question splits the whole zoo: did the bonds change, or only space?

segments.text: Let us open isomerism with a kitchen picture.
Two cooks get the exact same ingredients, in the same amounts. One makes a biryani, the other a pulao. Same shopping list, different dish, and a very different taste.
Isomers are exactly that: compounds with the same formula but a different arrangement of atoms, so their colour, melting point, and even reactivity all differ.
And the whole zoo of isomers splits cleanly on a single question: did the bonds change, or only the positions in space?
Look at the tree: on one side structural isomers, on the other stereoisomers, each with its own sub-types.
Structural isomers have different bonds. Something has moved between inside and outside the sphere, or a ligand is attached through a different atom.
Stereoisomers keep the very same bonds but a different arrangement in space. What is bonded to what does not change; only the geometry does.
So hold on to that one question. Did the bonds change, or only the space?
isomerism की शुरुआत एक kitchen picture से करते हैं।
दो cooks को बिलकुल same ingredients मिलते हैं, same amounts में। एक biryani बनाता है, दूसरा pulao। Same shopping list, अलग dish, और बहुत अलग taste.
Isomers बिलकुल यही हैं: compounds जिनका formula same है पर atoms का arrangement अलग, इसलिए उनका colour, melting point, और reactivity तक अलग होते हैं।
और isomers का पूरा zoo एक single सवाल पर साफ़-साफ़ बँट जाता है: bonds बदले, या सिर्फ space में positions?
tree देखो: एक तरफ़ structural isomers, दूसरी तरफ़ stereoisomers, हर एक के अपने sub-types.
Structural isomers में bonds अलग होते हैं। कुछ sphere के अंदर और बाहर के बीच move हुआ है, या कोई ligand अलग atom से attach है।
Stereoisomers वही bonds रखते हैं पर space में arrangement अलग। क्या किससे bonded है ये नहीं बदलता; सिर्फ geometry बदलती है।
तो वो एक सवाल पकड़कर रखो। Bonds बदले, या सिर्फ space?

sections.title: Geometrical isomerism: adjacent or opposite?

board_events.text: Cis, trans, and the fac and mer pair
Take an octahedral metal with four identical ligands and two chlorides. The two chlorides can sit adjacent, ninety degrees apart, or opposite, one hundred eighty degrees apart.

board_events.caption: cis, trans and the fac/mer arrangement

board_events.text: Adjacent gives the cis isomer, opposite gives the trans isomer $-$ same six bonds, different shape, and often a strikingly different colour.
When the split is three and three rather than four and two, the same idea gives the facial isomer, three like$-$ligands on one face, and the meridional isomer, spread around the middle.
The arrangement in space is everything $-$ that is the whole content of geometrical isomerism.
Never in tetrahedral $-$ every corner is a neighbour, so no cis versus trans exists
It also never appears at coordination number two or three, nor for the fully symmetric Ma6 or single$-$odd Ma5b.

segments.text: Geometrical isomerism is really about one thing: are two chosen ligands adjacent or opposite?
Take an octahedral metal with four identical ligands and two chlorides. The two chlorides can sit adjacent, ninety degrees apart, or opposite, one hundred eighty degrees apart.
Look at the octahedra: on the left the two special ligands are adjacent, in the middle they are opposite, and on the right the three-and-three split.
Adjacent gives the cis isomer, opposite gives the trans isomer. Same six bonds, a different shape, and very often a strikingly different colour.
When the split is three and three instead of four and two, the same idea gives the facial isomer, with three like ligands bunched on one face, and the meridional isomer, spread around the middle.
So the arrangement in space is everything. That really is the whole content of geometrical isomerism.
One firm rule: geometrical isomerism never occurs in tetrahedral complexes, because every corner is a neighbour, so there is no cis versus trans distinction.
It also never appears at coordination number two or three, nor for a fully symmetric M a six, nor for a single odd ligand M a five b.
Geometrical isomerism असल में एक ही चीज़ के बारे में है: दो chosen ligands adjacent हैं या opposite?
एक octahedral metal लो जिसमें चार identical ligands और दो chlorides हैं। दोनों chlorides adjacent बैठ सकते हैं, ninety degrees apart, या opposite, one hundred eighty degrees apart.
octahedra देखो: बाईं तरफ़ दोनों special ligands adjacent हैं, बीच में opposite, और दाईं तरफ़ three और three वाला split.
Adjacent देता है cis isomer, opposite देता है trans isomer. वही छह bonds, अलग shape, और अक्सर बहुत अलग colour.
जब split three और three होता है four और two की जगह, तो यही idea देता है facial isomer, तीन like ligands एक face पर बंचे हुए, और meridional isomer, बीच में फैले हुए।
तो space में arrangement ही सब कुछ है। यही असल में geometrical isomerism का पूरा content है।
एक पक्का rule: geometrical isomerism tetrahedral complexes में कभी नहीं होता, क्योंकि हर corner एक neighbour है, इसलिए cis versus trans का कोई distinction ही नहीं।
ये coordination number two या three पर भी कभी नहीं आता, ना fully symmetric M a six के लिए, ना single odd ligand M a five b के लिए।

sections.title: Optical isomerism: the hand-and-glove test

board_events.text: Non-superimposable mirror images
Hold up your two hands. They are mirror images, and no matter how you rotate one, it never lays perfectly on the other $-$ your right glove never fits your left hand.

board_events.text: Certain complexes are built the same way: their mirror image is non$-$superimposable. These are optical isomers, or enantiomers.
The two forms rotate plane$-$polarised light by equal amounts in opposite directions $-$ one to the right, called dextro or d, one to the left, called laevo or l.
A chiral complex is not missing anything compared with its mirror twin; both are perfectly valid, they are simply handed, like two spiral staircases winding opposite ways.
This handedness is most common in octahedral complexes carrying two or three chelate rings, because the chelate spans force a propeller$-$like twist no internal mirror can undo.
Racemic = a fifty$-$fifty d and l mixture giving zero net rotation; separating it is called resolution

segments.text: Optical isomerism is best felt with the hand and glove test.
Hold up your two hands. They are mirror images, and no matter how you rotate one, it never lays perfectly on the other. Your right glove simply never fits your left hand.
Look at this tris-chelate and its mirror image: try as you might, you cannot slide one onto the other.
Certain complexes are built the very same way: their mirror image is non superimposable. These are optical isomers, also called enantiomers.
The two forms rotate plane polarised light by equal amounts but in opposite directions. One turns it to the right, called dextro or d, the other to the left, called laevo or l.
A chiral complex is not missing anything compared with its mirror twin. Both are perfectly valid molecules; they are simply handed, like two spiral staircases winding in opposite ways.
This handedness is most common in octahedral complexes carrying two or three chelate rings, because the chelate spans force a propeller like twist that no internal mirror can undo.
A fifty fifty mixture of d and l is called racemic, and it gives zero net rotation because the two effects cancel. Separating it into pure d and l is called resolution.
Optical isomerism को hand और glove test से सबसे अच्छे से महसूस किया जाता है।
अपने दोनों हाथ उठाओ। ये mirror images हैं, और आप एक को कितना भी rotate करो, ये कभी दूसरे पर perfectly नहीं बैठता। आपका right glove left hand पर कभी fit नहीं होता।
इस tris-chelate और इसके mirror image को देखो: चाहे जितनी कोशिश करो, एक को दूसरे पर slide नहीं कर सकते।
कुछ complexes बिलकुल इसी तरह बने होते हैं: उनका mirror image non superimposable होता है। ये optical isomers हैं, जिन्हें enantiomers भी कहते हैं।
दोनों forms plane polarised light को equal amount पर opposite directions में rotate करती हैं। एक इसे right की ओर घुमाती है, dextro या d, दूसरी left की ओर, laevo या l.
एक chiral complex अपने mirror twin के मुक़ाबले कुछ भी missing नहीं है। दोनों perfectly valid molecules हैं; बस handed हैं, जैसे दो spiral staircases opposite directions में घूमती हुई।

ये handedness सबसे ज़्यादा octahedral complexes में मिलती है जिनमें दो या तीन chelate rings हों, क्योंकि chelate spans एक propeller जैसा twist force करते हैं जिसे कोई internal mirror undo नहीं कर सकता।
d और l का fifty fifty mixture racemic कहलाता है, और ये zero net rotation देता है क्योंकि दोनों effects cancel हो जाते हैं। इसे pure d और l में separate करना resolution कहलाता है।

board_events.caption: Linkage, ionisation, solvate and coordination isomerism

board_events.text: Ionisation isomerism: a counter ion and a coordinated ligand trade places, so the two isomers release different ions in solution and give different precipitation tests.

Solvate or hydrate isomerism: water sits inside the sphere in one isomer and as water of crystallisation outside in the other $-$ chromium chloride hexahydrate is the famous violet, grey$-$green, dark$-$green trio.
Coordination isomerism: in a salt of a complex cation and a complex anion, the ligands are distributed differently between the two metal centres.
These are not academic: the cis form of the platinum ammine chloride is the anticancer drug cisplatin, while the trans form is clinically useless.
Same atoms, same bonds, opposite spatial arrangement can mean completely different biology

segments.text: The structural family has four standard members, and each one ties back to an idea from the first sub-topic.

First, linkage isomerism: an ambidentate ligand binds through a different donor atom. Nitrite bound through nitrogen gives a yellow complex, while through oxygen the very same formula gives a red one.
Look at the four panels, each showing one structural type with its worked example.
Second, ionisation isomerism: a counter ion and a coordinated ligand trade places, so the two isomers release different ions in solution and give different precipitation tests.

Third, solvate or hydrate isomerism: water sits inside the sphere in one isomer and as water of crystallisation outside in the other. Chromium chloride hexahydrate is the famous trio, violet, grey green and dark green.
Fourth, coordination isomerism: in a salt made of a complex cation and a complex anion, the ligands are distributed differently between the two metal centres.
These distinctions are far from academic. The cis form of the platinum ammine chloride is the front line anticancer drug cisplatin, while the trans form is clinically useless.
Same atoms, same bonds, opposite spatial arrangement, and yet completely different biology.
structural family के चार standard members हैं, और हर एक first sub-topic के किसी idea से जुड़ता है।
पहला, linkage isomerism: एक ambidentate ligand अलग donor atom से बंधता है। Nitrite nitrogen से बंधकर yellow complex देता है, जबकि oxygen से वही formula red देता है।
चारों panels देखो, हर एक एक structural type अपने worked example के साथ दिखा रहा है।
दूसरा, ionisation isomerism: एक counter ion और एक coordinated ligand जगह बदल लेते हैं, इसलिए दोनों isomers solution में अलग ions release करते हैं और अलग precipitation tests देते हैं।

तीसरा, solvate या hydrate isomerism: एक isomer में water sphere के अंदर बैठता है और दूसरे में water of crystallisation की तरह बाहर। Chromium chloride hexahydrate famous trio है, violet, grey green और dark green.
चौथा, coordination isomerism: एक complex cation और complex anion से बने salt में, ligands दोनों metal centres के बीच अलग तरह से distribute होते हैं।
ये distinctions academic बिलकुल नहीं हैं। platinum ammine chloride का cis form front line anticancer drug cisplatin है, जबकि trans form clinically बेकार है।
same atoms, same bonds, opposite spatial arrangement, और फिर भी बिलकुल अलग biology.

board_events.caption: Fixing one ligand in Mabcd gives exactly three geometrical isomers

board_events.text: Octahedral shows geometrical isomerism for Ma4b2, Ma2b4, Ma4bc, and Ma3b3, which gives the facial and meridional pair $-$ but not for Ma6 or Ma5b.
For optical activity, a tris$-$chelate is always chiral, the cis form of a bis$-$chelate with two extra ligands is chiral, while its trans form is not.
Facial and meridional isomers are both optically inactive, and square planar complexes are almost always inactive because they keep a symmetry plane.
Train yourself to reason from the placement $-$ fix one ligand, ask what can sit opposite it $-$ and you never need to memorise an isomer$-$count table.
Optical activity is a pure symmetry question: no plane and no centre of symmetry means chiral

segments.text: Now the symmetry rules, which is exactly where marks quietly leak away.
Square planar shows geometrical isomerism for M a two b two, M a two b c, and M a b c d, which gives three isomers, but not for M a four, M a three b, or M a b three.
Look at the reasoning: in M a b c d, fix ligand a, then ask which of b, c or d sits opposite it. Three distinct choices, so exactly three isomers.
Octahedral shows geometrical isomerism for M a four b two, M a two b four, M a four b c, and M a three b three, the last giving the facial and meridional pair, but not for M a six or M a five b.
For optical activity, a tris chelate is always chiral, the cis form of a bis chelate with two extra ligands is chiral, while its trans form is not.
Facial and meridional isomers are both optically inactive, and square planar complexes are almost always inactive because they keep a symmetry plane.
Train yourself to reason from the placement. Fix one ligand, ask what can sit opposite it, and you will never need to memorise an isomer count table.
And keep the acid test in mind: optical activity is a pure symmetry question. No plane and no centre of symmetry means the complex is chiral.
अब symmetry rules, और यही वो जगह है जहाँ marks चुपचाप निकल जाते हैं।
Square planar geometrical isomerism दिखाता है M a two b two, M a two b c, और M a b c d के लिए, जो तीन isomers देता है, पर M a four, M a three b, या M a b three के लिए नहीं।
reasoning देखो: M a b c d में ligand a को fix करो, फिर पूछो कि b, c या d में से कौन इसके opposite बैठता है। तीन distinct choices, इसलिए exactly तीन isomers.

Octahedral geometrical isomerism दिखाता है M a four b two, M a two b four, M a four b c, और M a three b three के लिए, आखिरी वाला facial और meridional pair देता है, पर M a six या M a five b के लिए नहीं।
Optical activity के लिए, tris chelate हमेशा chiral होता है, दो extra ligands वाले bis chelate का cis form chiral होता है, जबकि उसका trans form नहीं।
Facial और meridional isomers दोनों optically inactive हैं, और square planar complexes लगभग हमेशा inactive होते हैं क्योंकि वो एक symmetry plane रखते हैं।
खुद को placement से reason करने की training दो। एक ligand fix करो, पूछो इसके opposite क्या बैठ सकता है, और फिर आपको कभी isomer count table रटने की ज़रूरत नहीं पड़ेगी।
और acid test याद रखो: optical activity एक pure symmetry सवाल है। कोई plane नहीं और कोई centre of symmetry नहीं, मतलब complex chiral है।

board_events.caption: cis and trans forms of the tetraamminedibromido ion

board_events.text: The two bromido ligands can sit cis, adjacent at ninety degrees, or trans, opposite at one hundred eighty degrees.
The cis isomer, with both bromides on one side, is polar with a non$-$zero dipole moment; the symmetric trans isomer has its bond dipoles cancelling.
That difference shows up in solubility and often in colour $-$ exactly the kind of point a board examiner expects you to mention alongside the drawing.
Names: cis- and trans-tetraamminedibromidochromium(III) ion

segments.text: This C B S E board example asks us to draw and name the geometrical isomers of an octahedral ion.
The coordination number is six, so the geometry is octahedral, and the skeleton is M a four b two, which does allow geometrical isomerism.
First the oxidation number: x plus four times zero plus two times minus one equals plus one, so chromium is plus three.
Look at the two drawings: on the left the cis form, on the right the trans form of the tetraamminedibromido ion.
The two bromido ligands can sit cis, adjacent at ninety degrees, or trans, opposite at one hundred eighty degrees.
The cis isomer, with both bromides on one side, is polar with a non zero dipole moment, while the symmetric trans isomer has its bond dipoles cancelling out.
That difference shows up in solubility and often in colour, which is exactly the kind of point a board examiner expects you to mention alongside the drawing.
The names are cis and trans tetraamminedibromidochromium three ion.
ये C B S E board example हमसे एक octahedral ion के geometrical isomers draw और name करने को कहता है।
Coordination number six है, तो geometry octahedral है, और skeleton M a four b two है, जो geometrical isomerism allow करता है।
पहले oxidation number: x plus four into zero plus two into minus one बराबर plus one, तो chromium है plus three.
दोनों drawings देखो: बाईं तरफ़ cis form, दाईं तरफ़ trans form, tetraamminedibromido ion का।
दोनों bromido ligands cis बैठ सकते हैं, adjacent ninety degrees पर, या trans, opposite one hundred eighty degrees पर।
cis isomer, जिसमें दोनों bromides एक side पर हैं, polar है non zero dipole moment के साथ, जबकि symmetric trans isomer में bond dipoles cancel हो जाते हैं।
ये difference solubility में और अक्सर colour में दिखता है, और यही वो point है जो board examiner drawing के साथ mention करने की उम्मीद करता है।
Names हैं cis और trans tetraamminedibromidochromium three ion.

The trap is picking the trans di$-$oxalato complex $-$ only the cis form of a bis$-$chelate is chiral, so read the cis or trans label before deciding.

segments.text: This N E E T speed trap asks which one of four complexes is optically active, and the trick is to scan, not draw.
The candidates are tris oxalato iron, trans di oxalato di aqua iron, hexammine nickel, and the square planar tetracyanonickelate.
Look at the four: three of them clearly carry a symmetry plane, while the tris chelate propeller does not.
Hexammine nickel is an M a six ion and the square planar ion both carry obvious symmetry planes, so both are optically inactive.
The trans arrangement of the two water ligands also sits on a mirror plane, so it too is inactive.
The tris chelate has no symmetry plane at all. It is the propeller shaped, always chiral case.
So the answer is the tris oxalato iron complex.
The classic trap is picking the trans di oxalato complex. Only the cis form of a bis chelate is chiral, so always read the cis or trans label before deciding.

sections.title: Worked example: linkage isomerism of [Cr(NH3)5(SCN)]2+

board_events.text: One ambidentate ligand, two isomers
The complex carries the ambidentate thiocyanate ligand, which can bind through sulphur, called thiocyanato$-$S, or through nitrogen, called isothiocyanato.

board_events.text: Because the same ligand can attach by a different atom, the complex therefore shows linkage isomerism.
The two names are pentaamminethiocyanato$-$S$-$chromium three ion and pentaamminethiocyanato$-$N$-$chromium three ion.
Now the second part: does it show geometrical isomerism? The skeleton is Ma5b, five ammonia and one thiocyanate.
A single odd ligand on an octahedron has only one possible position relative to the rest, so no geometrical isomerism is possible.
Ma5b: one odd ligand, one position, so no geometrical isomers

segments.text: This J E E Main example combines linkage isomerism, nomenclature and the ambidentate idea from the first sub-topic.
The complex carries the ambidentate thiocyanate ligand, which can bind through sulphur, called thiocyanato S, or through nitrogen, called isothiocyanato.
Look at the two structures: on the left thiocyanate binds through sulphur, on the right through nitrogen.
Because the same ligand can attach by a different atom, the complex therefore shows linkage isomerism.
The two names are pentaamminethiocyanato S chromium three ion and pentaamminethiocyanato N chromium three ion.
Now the second part of the question: does it show geometrical isomerism? The skeleton here is M a five b, five ammonia and one thiocyanate.
A single odd ligand on an octahedron has only one possible position relative to all the rest, so no geometrical isomerism is possible.
So remember, for M a five b there is one odd ligand, one position, and therefore no geometrical isomers.
ये J E E Main example linkage isomerism, nomenclature और first sub-topic वाले ambidentate idea को combine करता है।
complex में ambidentate thiocyanate ligand है, जो sulphur से बंध सकता है, thiocyanato S, या nitrogen से, isothiocyanato.
दोनों structures देखो: बाईं तरफ़ thiocyanate sulphur से बंधता है, दाईं तरफ़ nitrogen से।
क्योंकि same ligand अलग atom से attach हो सकता है, इसलिए complex linkage isomerism दिखाता है।
दोनों names हैं pentaamminethiocyanato S chromium three ion और pentaamminethiocyanato N chromium three ion.
अब सवाल का दूसरा हिस्सा: क्या ये geometrical isomerism दिखाता है? यहाँ skeleton M a five b है, पाँच ammonia और एक thiocyanate.
एक octahedron पर single odd ligand की बाकी सबके relative सिर्फ एक ही possible position होती है, इसलिए geometrical isomerism possible ही नहीं।
तो याद रखो, M a five b के लिए एक odd ligand, एक position, और इसलिए कोई geometrical isomers नहीं।

board_events.text: Step one, the geometrical isomers: the ammonia and chloride sit either cis or trans, while the two en units bridge the remaining positions.

segments.text: This J E E Advanced example is the full stereoisomer count, and it shows the standard layering trap.
First the checks: cobalt comes out plus three, and the coordination number is two times two, plus one, plus one, which is six, so it is octahedral.
The skeleton is a bis chelate with two extra different ligands. The two monodentate ligands, ammonia and chloride, can be cis or trans to each other.
Look at the three structures: one trans on the left, and the cis form drawn as a mirror image pair on the right.
Step one, the geometrical isomers: the ammonia and chloride sit either cis or trans, while the two en units bridge the remaining positions.
Step two, test each one for chirality. The trans isomer has a plane of symmetry, so it is optically inactive, a single structure.
The cis isomer has no symmetry plane, so it is chiral, existing as a non superimposable d and l pair.
So the total is three stereoisomers: one trans, which is achiral, plus a cis d and l pair. Doing the geometrical layer before the optical layer is what stops you dropping a hidden enantiomer.
ये J E E Advanced example full stereoisomer count है, और ये standard layering trap दिखाता है।
पहले checks: cobalt निकलता है plus three, और coordination number है two into two, plus one, plus one, यानी six, तो ये octahedral है।
Skeleton एक bis chelate है दो extra different ligands के साथ। दोनों monodentate ligands, ammonia और chloride, एक-दूसरे के cis या trans हो सकते हैं।
तीनों structures देखो: बाईं तरफ़ एक trans, और दाईं तरफ़ cis form एक mirror image pair की तरह।
Step one, geometrical isomers: ammonia और chloride या तो cis या trans बैठते हैं, जबकि दोनों en units बाकी positions को bridge करती हैं।
Step two, हर एक की chirality test करो। trans isomer में plane of symmetry है, इसलिए वो optically inactive है, एक single structure.
cis isomer में कोई symmetry plane नहीं, इसलिए वो chiral है, एक non superimposable d और l pair की तरह exist करता है।
तो total है तीन stereoisomers: एक trans, जो achiral है, plus एक cis d और l pair। Optical layer से पहले geometrical layer करना ही आपको एक hidden enantiomer छोड़ने से बचाता है।

sections.title: Pitfalls and pro-tips for isomerism

board_events.text: The classic isomerism traps
Claiming geometrical isomerism for tetrahedral complexes: an Ma2b2 formula shows cis and trans only if it is square planar; in a tetrahedron every position is adjacent.
Assuming any didentate complex is optically active: for a bis$-$chelate with two extra ligands, only the cis isomer is chiral, while the trans keeps a symmetry plane.
A chelate ring by itself is not proof of chirality $-$ check the cis or trans label first
Confusing ionisation with solvate isomerism: both swap with the lattice, but ionisation swaps an ionic ligand with a counter ion, while solvate swaps a water ligand with water of crystallisation.
Counting geometrical isomers but forgetting the optical layer: when asked for stereoisomers, test each geometrical isomer for chirality and add a d and l pair wherever there is no symmetry plane.
Pro$-$tip: for optical activity hunt for the plane of symmetry before drawing; for counting, lock the geometrical count first and only then sprinkle optical pairs on top.

segments.text: Let us close isomerism with the classic traps that catch students out.

First, claiming geometrical isomerism for tetrahedral complexes. An M a two b two formula shows cis and trans only if it is square planar; in a tetrahedron every position is adjacent, so there is no cis versus trans.
Second, assuming any didentate complex is optically active. For a bis chelate with two extra ligands, only the cis isomer is chiral, while the trans keeps a symmetry plane and is inactive.
Remember, a chelate ring by itself is not proof of chirality. Always check the cis or trans label first.

Third, confusing ionisation with solvate isomerism. Both involve a swap with the lattice, but ionisation swaps an ionic ligand with a counter ion, while solvate swaps a water ligand with water of crystallisation.

Fourth, counting geometrical isomers but forgetting the optical layer. When asked for stereoisomers, test each geometrical isomer for chirality and add a d and l pair wherever there is no symmetry plane.
And the pro tip: for optical activity, hunt for the plane of symmetry before you draw; for counting, lock the geometrical count first and only then sprinkle the optical pairs on top.
isomerism को उन classic traps के साथ खत्म करते हैं जो students को फँसाते हैं।

पहला, tetrahedral complexes के लिए geometrical isomerism claim करना। एक M a two b two formula cis और trans तभी दिखाता है जब वो square planar हो; tetrahedron में हर position adjacent है, इसलिए कोई cis versus trans नहीं।

दूसरा, ये मान लेना कि कोई भी didentate complex optically active है। दो extra ligands वाले bis chelate के लिए, सिर्फ cis isomer chiral होता है, जबकि trans एक symmetry plane रखता है और inactive होता है।
याद रखो, chelate ring अकेले chirality का proof नहीं है। हमेशा पहले cis या trans label check करो।

तीसरा, ionisation को solvate isomerism से confuse करना। दोनों में lattice के साथ swap होता है, पर ionisation एक ionic ligand को counter ion से swap करता है, जबकि solvate एक water ligand को water of crystallisation से।
चौथा, geometrical isomers गिनना पर optical layer भूल जाना। जब stereoisomers पूछे जाएँ, हर geometrical isomer की chirality test करो और जहाँ कोई symmetry plane नहीं वहाँ एक d और l pair जोड़ो।
और pro tip: optical activity के लिए, draw करने से पहले plane of symmetry ढूँढो; counting के लिए, पहले geometrical count lock करो और तभी उसके ऊपर optical pairs छिड़को।

sections.title: Valence Bond Theory: the metal opens rooms for guests

board_events.text: Why is one complex magnetic and another not?
Werner could count coordination numbers, but he was silent on colour and magnetism. To explain those we need a picture of the actual bonding.
Think of the metal ion as a hotel with vacant rooms $-$ empty orbitals. Each ligand arrives with its own lone pair and is given a room.
First the hotel merges a specific set of empty orbitals into new, identical rooms all pointing the right way; this merging is hybridisation, and its shape is the geometry.

board_events.text: If the metal uses inner $n$ minus one d orbitals it must shove its own electrons together first, giving an inner$-$orbital, low$-$spin complex, d2sp3.
If it reaches for the outer $n$d orbitals and leaves its electrons undisturbed, it gives an outer$-$orbital, high$-$spin complex, sp3d2.
Inner orbital = low spin (electrons paired); outer orbital = high spin (electrons left unpaired)

segments.text: <curious>Here is the question Werner could not answer:</curious> why is one complex strongly magnetic and a similar one not?
Werner could count coordination numbers, but he stayed silent on colour and magnetism. To explain those, we need a picture of the actual bonding.
Think of the metal ion as a hotel with vacant rooms, meaning empty orbitals. Each ligand arrives carrying its own lone pair and is handed a room.
But first the hotel merges a specific set of empty orbitals into new, identical rooms all pointing the right way. This merging is hybridisation, and the shape of that hybrid set is the geometry.
Look at the two fillings: on top the inner orbital case with electrons paired, below the outer orbital case with electrons left alone.
If the metal uses its inner n minus one d orbitals, it must first shove its own electrons together, giving an inner orbital, low spin complex, d two s p three.
If instead it reaches for the outer n d orbitals and leaves its own electrons undisturbed, it gives an outer orbital, high spin complex, s p three d two.
So hold this dictionary: inner orbital means low spin with electrons paired, and outer orbital means high spin with electrons left unpaired.
<curious>ये वो सवाल है जो Werner नहीं समझा सका:</curious> एक complex strongly magnetic क्यों है और एक similar वाला नहीं?
Werner coordination numbers गिन सकता था, पर colour और magnetism पर चुप था। इन्हें explain करने के लिए हमें असली bonding की एक picture चाहिए।
metal ion को एक hotel समझो जिसमें vacant rooms हैं, यानी empty orbitals. हर ligand अपना lone pair लेकर आता है और उसे एक room दे दिया जाता है।
पर पहले hotel empty orbitals के एक specific set को merge करके नए identical rooms बनाता है, सब सही direction में pointing. यही merging hybridisation है, और उस hybrid set का shape ही geometry है।
दोनों fillings देखो: ऊपर inner orbital case electrons paired के साथ, नीचे outer orbital case electrons अकेले छोड़े हुए।
अगर metal अपने inner n minus one d orbitals use करता है, तो उसे पहले अपने electrons साथ धकेलने पड़ते हैं, जिससे inner orbital, low spin complex बनता है, d two s p three.
और अगर वो outer n d orbitals की तरफ़ जाता है और अपने electrons को undisturbed छोड़ देता है, तो outer orbital, high spin complex बनता है, s p three d two.
तो ये dictionary पकड़ो: inner orbital मतलब low spin electrons paired के साथ, और outer orbital मतलब high spin electrons unpaired के साथ।

sections.title: Crystal Field Theory: point charges push on shelves

board_events.text: Ligands as point charges that split the d-orbitals
Crystal Field Theory throws away shared pairs and treats every ligand as a point negative charge that repels the metal's d electrons.
In a free metal ion the five d orbitals are degenerate $-$ five shelves at the same height.

board_events.text: Surround the ion with ligands in a definite geometry and the shelves no longer stay level: orbitals pointing at the ligands rise, those pointing between them drop.
In an octahedral field the two orbitals aimed along the axes rise into the higher e g set, and the three aimed between the axes drop into the lower t two g set.
The gap between them is the crystal field splitting energy, $\Delta_o$ $-$ colour, magnetism and stability all flow from its size
The split is barycentric: the three t two g orbitals drop by nought point four, the two e g rise by nought point six, so the average energy is unchanged.

segments.text: Now the second picture, Crystal Field Theory, which treats the ligands as point charges pushing on shelves.
Crystal Field Theory throws away the idea of shared electron pairs and treats every ligand as a point negative charge that repels the metal's d electrons.
In a free metal ion the five d orbitals are degenerate, like five shelves sitting at exactly the same height.
Look at the splitting diagram: the five degenerate orbitals separate into a lower group and an upper group.
Surround the ion with ligands in a definite geometry and the shelves no longer stay level. Orbitals pointing straight at the ligands are pushed up, while those pointing between the ligands drop down.
In an octahedral field, the two orbitals aimed along the axes rise into the higher e g set, and the three aimed between the axes drop into the lower t two g set.
The gap between them is the crystal field splitting energy, delta O, and everything downstream, colour, magnetism and stability, flows from the size of this one gap.
The split is barycentric: the three t two g orbitals drop by nought point four delta O, the two e g rise by nought point six, so the average energy stays unchanged.
अब दूसरी picture, Crystal Field Theory, जो ligands को point charges मानती है जो shelves पर push करते हैं।
Crystal Field Theory shared electron pairs का idea छोड़ देती है और हर ligand को एक point negative charge मानती है जो metal के d electrons को repel करता है।
एक free metal ion में पाँचों d orbitals degenerate होते हैं, जैसे पाँच shelves बिलकुल same height पर।
splitting diagram देखो: पाँच degenerate orbitals एक lower group और एक upper group में अलग हो जाते हैं।

ion को ligands से एक definite geometry में घेरो और shelves level नहीं रहतीं। जो orbitals सीधे ligands की तरफ़ point करते हैं वो ऊपर धकेले जाते हैं, और जो ligands के बीच point करते हैं वो नीचे गिरते हैं।
एक octahedral field में, axes के साथ aim करने वाले दो orbitals ऊपर higher e g set में जाते हैं, और axes के बीच aim करने वाले तीन नीचे lower t two g set में गिरते हैं।
इनके बीच का gap crystal field splitting energy है, delta O, और इसके बाद सब कुछ, colour, magnetism और stability, इसी एक gap के size से बहता है।
split barycentric है: तीन t two g orbitals नौंट point four delta O गिरते हैं, दो e g नौंट point six ऊपर उठते हैं, तो average energy unchanged रहती है।

sections.title: Square planar, tetrahedral, and the colour of Ti(III)

board_events.text: Two more geometries, and where colour comes from
Square planar is an octahedron with the two $z$-axis ligands pulled away: the $z$-component orbitals sink, leaving $d_{x^2-y^2}$ alone at the top.

In a tetrahedral field the splitting inverts, with the $e$ set below the $t_2$ set, and it is much smaller, only four ninths of $\Delta_o$ $-$ so tetrahedral complexes are always high spin.

board_events.text: Take the titanium three aqua ion, a d one system with its one electron in t two g. It absorbs blue$-$green light to promote that electron up to e g.
The absorbed energy is exactly $\Delta_o$, and the eye sees the complement of what was absorbed, so the ion looks violet.
Observed colour = complement of the absorbed d$-$d transition, whose energy is $\Delta_o$

segments.text: Now two more geometries, and the place colour actually comes from.
Square planar is best seen as an octahedron with the two ligands on the z axis pulled away. The orbitals with a z component sink, leaving d x squared minus y squared alone at the top.
Look at the two panels: on the left the square planar levels, on the right the inverted tetrahedral field.
That is exactly why a d eight ion with a strong field ligand prefers square planar. The lone high orbital can be left empty and every electron paired.
In a tetrahedral field the splitting inverts, with the e set below the t two set, and it is much smaller, only four ninths of delta O, so tetrahedral complexes are always high spin.
Now look at this colour picture: a d one ion absorbs one photon and shows its complement.
Take the titanium three aqua ion, a d one system with its single electron sitting in t two g. It absorbs blue green light to promote that electron up into e g.
The absorbed energy is exactly delta O, and the eye sees the complement of what was absorbed, so the ion looks violet.
So the observed colour is always the complement of that d to d transition, and the energy of the transition is exactly delta O.
अब दो और geometries, और वो जगह जहाँ से colour असल में आता है।
Square planar को एक octahedron की तरह देखो जिसमें z axis वाले दो ligands खींच लिए गए हों। z component वाले orbitals नीचे बैठ जाते हैं, और d x squared minus y squared अकेला ऊपर रह जाता है।
दोनों panels देखो: बाईं तरफ़ square planar levels, दाईं तरफ़ inverted tetrahedral field.
यही वजह है कि एक d eight ion strong field ligand के साथ square planar prefer करता है। वो lone high orbital empty छोड़ा जा सकता है और हर electron paired.
एक tetrahedral field में splitting invert हो जाती है, e set t two set के नीचे, और ये बहुत छोटी होती है, सिर्फ़ four ninths of delta O, इसलिए tetrahedral complexes हमेशा high spin होते हैं।
अब ये colour picture देखो: एक d one ion एक photon absorb करता है और अपना complement दिखाता है।
titanium three aqua ion लो, एक d one system जिसका single electron t two g में बैठा है। ये blue green light absorb करके उस electron को e g में promote करता है।
absorbed energy exactly delta O है, और आँख absorbed का complement देखती है, इसलिए ion violet दिखता है।
तो observed colour हमेशा उस d to d transition का complement होता है, और transition की energy exactly delta O होती है।

board_events.text: The useful values are worth memorising: one, two, three, four and five unpaired electrons give one point seven three, two point eight three, three point eight seven, four point nine zero and five point nine two Bohr Magneton.

board_events.latex: \text{CN }6:\ d^2sp^3\,(\text{inner, low spin})\ \text{or}\ sp^3d^2\,(\text{outer, high spin})

board_events.text: The number of leftover unpaired electrons is exactly what a magnetic balance measures, so this single formula ties a structural choice to a real number.
The reasoning chain: oxidation number, then $d^n$, then ligand field, then spin, then unpaired count, then $\mu$

segments.text: Let us gather the Valence Bond toolkit: hybridisation by coordination number, and the spin only magnetic moment.
The spin only moment is mu equals root n into n plus two Bohr Magneton, where n is the number of unpaired electrons.
Look at the bar chart: the moment climbs steadily as the unpaired count rises.

The useful values are worth memorising: one, two, three, four and five unpaired electrons give one point seven three, two point eight three, three point eight seven, four point nine zero, and five point nine two Bohr Magneton.
For coordination number six, the hybridisation is d two s p three, the inner orbital low spin case, or s p three d two, the outer orbital high spin case.
For coordination number four, it is d s p two for square planar, or s p three for tetrahedral.
The number of leftover unpaired electrons is exactly what a magnetic balance measures, so this one formula ties a structural choice directly to a real, measurable number.
And hold the reasoning chain: oxidation number, then the d n count, then the ligand field strength, then high or low spin, then the unpaired count, and finally mu.
अब Valence Bond toolkit इकट्ठा करते हैं: coordination number से hybridisation, और spin only magnetic moment.
spin only moment है mu बराबर root n into n plus two Bohr Magneton, जहाँ n unpaired electrons की संख्या है।
bar chart देखो: unpaired count बढ़ने के साथ moment steadily चढ़ता है।

useful values याद रखने लायक हैं: one, two, three, four और five unpaired electrons देते हैं one point seven three, two point eight three, three point eight seven, four point nine zero, और five point nine two Bohr Magneton.
coordination number six के लिए hybridisation है d two s p three, inner orbital low spin case, या s p three d two, outer orbital high spin case.
coordination number four के लिए, d s p two square planar के लिए, या s p three tetrahedral के लिए।
बचे हुए unpaired electrons की संख्या exactly वही है जो magnetic balance measure करता है, तो ये एक formula एक structural choice को सीधे एक real measurable number से जोड़ देता है।
और reasoning chain पकड़ो: oxidation number, फिर d n count, फिर ligand field strength, फिर high या low spin, फिर unpaired count, और आख़िर में mu.

sections.title: The CFT toolkit: splitting, CFSE, spin and colour

board_events.text: Energies, stabilisation, spin criterion and the series
A more negative CFSE means a more stable arrangement; $m$ is the number of extra paired electrons relative to the free ion, and $P$ is the pairing energy.
Only octahedral d four to d seven ions face a high$-$versus$-$low$-$spin choice at all; everywhere else the filling is forced.

board_events.text: Bigger field means bigger $\Delta_o$ means shorter absorbed wavelength; observed colour is the complement

segments.text: Now the Crystal Field toolkit: the splitting energies, stabilisation, the spin criterion and the series.
The e g orbitals sit at plus nought point six delta O and the t two g at minus nought point four delta O, while the tetrahedral gap is four ninths of delta O.
The crystal field stabilisation energy is minus nought point four times the t two g count plus nought point six times the e g count, all times delta O, plus an m P term.
A more negative crystal field stabilisation energy means a more stable arrangement. Here m is the number of extra paired electrons relative to the free ion, and P is the pairing energy.
The spin criterion is simple: if delta O is greater than P you get low spin, and if delta O is less than P you get high spin.
Only octahedral d four to d seven ions face a high versus low spin choice at all. Everywhere else the filling is forced.
And the colour link: delta O equals the absorbed energy, which is h c over lambda.
Look at the spectrochemical series running from weak field on the left to strong field on the right.
So a bigger field means a bigger splitting, which means a shorter absorbed wavelength, and the observed colour is always the complement.
अब Crystal Field toolkit: splitting energies, stabilisation, spin criterion और series.
e g orbitals plus नौंट point six delta O पर बैठते हैं और t two g minus नौंट point four delta O पर, जबकि tetrahedral gap four ninths of delta O है।
crystal field stabilisation energy है minus नौंट point four गुना t two g count plus नौंट point six गुना e g count, सब गुना delta O, plus एक m P term.
ज़्यादा negative crystal field stabilisation energy मतलब ज़्यादा stable arrangement. यहाँ m free ion के मुक़ाबले extra paired electrons की संख्या है, और P pairing energy है।
spin criterion simple है: अगर delta O, P से बड़ा है तो low spin मिलता है, और अगर delta O, P से छोटा है तो high spin.
सिर्फ़ octahedral d four से d seven ions के पास high versus low spin का choice होता है। बाकी हर जगह filling forced है।
और colour link: delta O बराबर है absorbed energy, यानी h c over lambda.
spectrochemical series देखो जो बाईं तरफ़ weak field से दाईं तरफ़ strong field तक जाती है।
तो बड़ा field मतलब बड़ा splitting, यानी छोटा absorbed wavelength, और observed colour हमेशा complement होता है।

board_events.text: Hybridisation, geometry and magnetic moment
First the oxidation number: chromium plus six times zero equals plus three, so we have chromium three, configuration three d three.

board_events.text: The coordination number is six, so the geometry is octahedral, and with only three d electrons each sits in its own orbital by Hund's rule.

Three unpaired electrons, so the complex is paramagnetic

segments.text: This C B S E level example asks for the hybridisation, geometry and spin only moment using Valence Bond Theory.
First the oxidation number: chromium plus six times zero equals plus three, so we have chromium three, with configuration three d three.
Look at the filling: three d electrons, three unpaired, and two inner d orbitals left free.
The coordination number is six, so the geometry is octahedral, and with only three d electrons each one sits in its own orbital by Hund's rule.
Two inner three d orbitals are already empty, so here no pairing decision is even needed.
The hybridisation is therefore d two s p three, the inner orbital octahedral case.
The moment is root of three into three plus two, which is root fifteen, giving three point eight seven Bohr Magneton.
With three unpaired electrons, the complex is paramagnetic.
ये C B S E level example Valence Bond Theory से hybridisation, geometry और spin only moment पूछता है।
पहले oxidation number: chromium plus six into zero बराबर plus three, तो हमारे पास chromium three है, configuration three d three के साथ।
filling देखो: तीन d electrons, तीन unpaired, और दो inner d orbitals free.
coordination number six है, तो geometry octahedral है, और सिर्फ़ तीन d electrons के साथ हर एक Hund's rule से अपने orbital में बैठता है।
दो inner three d orbitals पहले से empty हैं, तो यहाँ कोई pairing decision लेने की ज़रूरत ही नहीं।
इसलिए hybridisation है d two s p three, inner orbital octahedral case.
moment है root of three into three plus two, यानी root fifteen, जो देता है three point eight seven Bohr Magneton.
तीन unpaired electrons के साथ, complex paramagnetic है।

sections.title: Worked example: highest magnetic moment among aqua complexes

board_events.text: Weak field means count unpaired straight from d-count
The candidates are the hexa$-$aqua complexes of manganese two, iron two, cobalt two and nickel two.

segments.text: This N E E T speed trap asks which hexa aqua complex has the highest spin only moment.
The candidates are the hexa aqua complexes of manganese two, iron two, cobalt two and nickel two.
Look at the bar chart of unpaired counts for each of the four aqua ions.
The speed logic: water is a weak field ligand, sitting low in the series, so every one of these is high spin, and we count unpaired electrons straight from the d count.
Manganese two is d five with five unpaired, iron two is d six with four, cobalt two is d seven with three, and nickel two is d eight with two.
The highest unpaired count belongs to manganese two, so it has the largest magnetic moment.

segments.text: This J E E Main example computes the crystal field stabilisation energy for two iron complexes, one with a weak ligand and one with a strong one.
Both the hexa aqua and the hexacyanido iron complexes are iron two, so both are d six.
Look at the two fillings: high spin d six on the left, low spin d six on the right.
Water is a weak field ligand, giving high spin t two g four e g two.
Its stabilisation energy is minus nought point four times four plus nought point six times two, all times delta O, which is minus nought point four delta O.
Cyanide is a strong field ligand, giving low spin t two g six e g zero.

Its stabilisation energy is minus nought point four times six plus nought point six times zero, all times delta O, which is minus two point four delta O, plus a pairing penalty for the two extra pairs.
The cyanide complex has a far more negative stabilisation energy, so it is much more strongly stabilised, which fits cyanide sitting high in the spectrochemical series.
